newsitem.title: GERMANY: Don't forget the Berlin Wall say campaigners.
newsitem.headline: Don't forget the Berlin Wall say campaigners.

text.p: Berlin archivists, artists and politicians called on Monday for a concerted effort to protect the last remaining fragments of the Berlin Wall from property developers, trophy hunters and the weather.
"There is hardly anything left of this piece of global history," said Rainer Hildebrandt, director of the Haus am Checkpoint Charlie museum at the former Allied border crossing.

"People want to be able to touch this thing that divided the world," Hildebrandt told a news conference to present the annual report of the August 13 Working Group, which campaigns to make sure the Wall and its victims are not forgotton.
"This Wall was not just the Wall of Berlin, but of Europe and the whole world," he said.

The barricade, erected on August 13, 1961, split the city for nearly 30 years until the collapse of communism in 1989, a year before German unification, but was quickly torn down and has now almost disappeared.
Many want the last standing fragments -- adding up to less than one kilometre of the original 42-km (26-mile) Wall -- to be preserved as a political symbol and tourist attraction.

"Everybody asks us where was the Wall. But what we need to ask is what was the Wall and what happened on the Wall," Hagen Koch, an archivist, told journalists. "We have to remember because of the tragedies that happened there."
Evidence gathered by the August 13 group from East German files, relatives and witnesses suggests at least 916 people died trying to flee from old communist East Germany.

About 255 of them were killed in attempts to escape over the Wall from East Berlin into West Berlin, then an enclave sealed off from surrounding East Germany by the concrete barrier. Many victims were shot by East German border guards.
No reliable official figures are available because East Germany did not keep records of border deaths.
Tourists were split on how much of the wall should stay.
Colin Stainton, a tourist from England, said he was disappointed so little of the hated barricade still stood.
"It carries a message for all of us," he said. "It's a shame that young people are coming here and chipping away at it -- they don't know the significance of what they're doing.
But Ria Conings, a visitor from Belgium, said one short section was enough to remind people of the divided city.
"People in Berlin have had to live with this wall for too long. It represents the past and I think it's right that it should go," she said.

Hildebrandt's August 13 group, however, are determined to protect the remaining 10 sections and mark the former route of the whole barricade with cobble stones spelling out the words "The Wall" in several different languages.

The cash-strapped Berlin city government has struggled to finance renovation work on the remaining pieces and last year said it would settle for a marker in red paint along one section until it can afford a more lasting symbol.

Hildebrandt is particularly upset about the removal of Wall segments by developers at the Potsdamer Platz -- the square at the heart of pre-war Berlin now being re-made as a shopping, business and entertainment paradise.
The museum director said he was even fighting to keep the famous Checkpoint Charlie sign announcing "You are leaving the American Sector" of (West) Berlin in its original position.
"The designers of the new building next to us say it spoils the architecture," he said.
